text.en: Something is wrong. A child's rangoli does not look like Amma's rangoli. Amma made a pretty one with dots and shapes. Let us make it on paper too, and then use shapes, boxes, matchsticks and paper plates to find out what makes a square a square, a rectangle a rectangle, a triangle a triangle and a circle a circle.

We begin with Amma's rangoli. It is made by joining dots, and when we join them we get shapes that we can name. In the rangoli we see shapes such as a square, a triangle and a circle. Some shapes are drawn with curved lines and some with straight lines, so we count both kinds. We can also make a rangoli by laying shape cut-outs on paper, drawing round them and colouring. Two children can compare their rangolis and talk about what is the same and what is different. Shapes are all around us, so looking carefully at them is the first step in this chapter.
Collect a cardboard box and open it out carefully. Every flat part of the box is called a face, and when the box is opened we see the faces as flat shapes. Most of them are rectangles, and some may be squares. We can use the opened box to make a gift box for Diwali sweets, and we can fold a square paper to make an envelope for a card. When we trace the faces of a cuboid, such as an eraser or a matchbox, on paper we get rectangles, and sometimes squares. A cuboid can never have a face that is a triangle. Different children tracing different faces of the same matchbox may get different rectangles, because the faces of a matchbox are not all the same size.
A rectangle has 4 sides and 4 corners. We can build one by joining four sticks. In a rectangle the opposite sides are equal in length. This does not mean all four sides must be equal. A long rectangle and a short rectangle are both rectangles. A rectangle can be small or big and can be drawn in many positions, for example standing up, lying down or tilted on a dot grid. It is still the same kind of shape. When biscuits are packed in a box they fit well together because their faces are all rectangular and the same size. Objects like a book, a door, a blackboard and a notebook have rectangular faces. To find rectangles in a picture we count carefully, because small rectangles can join to make bigger rectangles, so there may be more rectangles than we first see.
Chess boards, ludo boards and floor tiles are square in shape. If we fold a square tile in half it becomes a rectangle, so the two shapes are close relatives. Both a square and a rectangle have 4 sides and 4 corners. That is what is the same. The difference is in the sides. In a rectangle only the opposite sides must be equal. In a square all four sides must be equal in length. We can make a square with four matchsticks of the same length. We can also draw bigger and bigger squares around a small square on a dot grid, and squares can be joined to make new shapes.
Look at the corner of a tile, a table or a maths book. Such a corner is called a square corner. To check a corner, pile one square over another, or one rectangle over another. The corners fit exactly on top of each other, so all the corners of a square and of a rectangle are square corners. We can join two paper strips to show three kinds of corner: one smaller than a square corner, one exactly a square corner and one bigger than a square corner. This strip also tells us whether the corner of our desk or the board is a square corner. Some shapes have only square corners, some have corners smaller than a square corner and some have corners bigger than a square corner, and one shape can have more than one kind.
Look at a slice of pizza, a roof end, a flag, a sandwich cut diagonally and a set square. All of them have triangular faces. A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners. We can find many triangles hidden inside one rangoli, so we count one by one with care. We can build triangles with sticks and clay and by folding and cutting paper. Moving just two matchsticks can turn one triangle into two triangles, which shows how shapes can be changed by moving their sides.
Bottle caps, bangles, rings, coins and the wheels of a circus cycle are like circles. A circle is round and has no corners and no straight sides. Take a paper plate and fold it in half. The fold is a straight line through the circle. Fold it in another way and we get another straight line, and these lines meet at one point. The point where the folds meet is the centre of the circle. We can draw a circle by tracing a bottle cap, a bangle or a ring, or by marking a circle on the ground for a game. We can also make puppets using circular shapes.
To compare two shapes we look at how many sides they have, how many corners they have, and whether the sides are straight or curved. A square and a triangle both have straight sides but not the same number of sides or corners. In an odd-one-out puzzle, any shape can be the odd one if we can give a good reason, so we must explain why. Borders on sarees, doors and flower decorations are made from straight and curved lines. We can make our own border and continue a line pattern. A tangram is a puzzle of seven pieces, made of triangles and a square and another four-sided shape. We can arrange them to make new pictures.

problem.en: Murugan made three squares in a row with 10 matchsticks. With 12 matchsticks, what is the most number of squares he can see?

text.en: Make three squares in a row. They share their middle sides, so they use 4 + 3 + 3 = 10 sticks.

why.en: Squares that touch share a side, so we need fewer sticks than 4 for each square.

text.en: With 12 matchsticks make a block of two rows and two columns. It has 4 small squares.

why.en: This block uses 12 sticks and is closed on all sides.

text.en: Look again at the whole block: the four small squares together make one big square, which is a 5th square.

why.en: Counting both small and big squares gives 4 + 1 = 5 squares.

problem.en: How do we find the centre of a paper plate (a circle)?

text.en: Fold the plate in half so the edges meet. Open it and mark the fold line.

why.en: The fold line is a straight line through the circle.

text.en: Fold the plate in half again in a different way and mark the second line.

why.en: Two different folds give two different straight lines.

text.en: Look where the two lines meet. That meeting point is the centre of the circle.

why.en: Every fold of this kind passes through the centre.

problem.en: Is the corner of our tile a square corner? How do we check it with two paper strips?

text.en: Join two paper strips at one end so that they make a corner we can open and close.

why.en: The strips act as a corner that can be changed.

text.en: Place the strip corner in a square corner of the tile and open it until it fits the corner exactly. This is a square corner.

why.en: A square corner is the corner that fits exactly.

text.en: Now place it on the table corner. If it fits exactly, that corner is also a square corner. If there is a gap, it is smaller or bigger.

why.en: This gives us a simple tool to check corners.

prompt.en: Tell a friend how a square and a rectangle are the same and how they are different, and how to check a square corner.

requiredIdeas.en: In a square all four sides are equal, but in a rectangle only opposite sides are equal
All corners of both are square corners that can be checked by fitting a paper strip corner

commonMisconceptions.en: A rectangle must be long and thin
Only a square has square corners

points.en: A rectangle has 4 sides and 4 corners, with opposite sides equal in length.
A square is special because all 4 of its sides are equal.
All corners of a square and of a rectangle are square corners, and a paper strip corner can check them.
A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners.
A circle is round, has no corners and no straight sides, and its folds meet at the centre.
Shapes can be compared by sides, corners and whether the lines are straight or curved.
